samples.summary: `Secure`/`__Host-` on session, refresh, OAuth-state and CLI-confirm cookies is now dropped on any `NODE_ENV=production` deployment whose `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starts with `http://` — the exact shape produced by a TLS-terminating proxy in front of the backend. This is a fail-open regression from the previous unconditional `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`.
samples.evidence: `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:229-240) returns `false` for any callback URL beginning `http://`, *before* the `NODE_ENV === 'production'` fallback is reached. `auth.controller.ts:406` now feeds that answer into `baseCookieOptions()` for the session and refresh cookies, where the diff removed `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`. Both `packages/backend/README.md:41` and `packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42` hand operators `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://…`, and `ConfigModule.forRoot()` loads `.env` into `process.env`, so a production self-host behind an https edge that never re-pointed the callback URL will (a) transmit the session and refresh JWTs without `Secure`, so any plaintext hop to the same host (an http→https redirect, a mixed-content subresource) leaks them, and (b) lose the `__Host-` prefix this very change added, so the sibling-subdomain session-planting it claims to close stays open on those installs. `COOKIE_SECURE=true` and the new one-line warning (`github-auth.guard.ts:263`) are opt-in mitigations, not defaults; the safe default when `NODE_ENV=production` would be to keep `Secure` and require an explicit opt-out.

samples.summary: `cliLoginAvailable()` accepts a loopback callback host as "positive evidence that the consent cookie can be trusted", but on a loopback deployment `useSecureCookies()` is false, so `wafflebase_cli_confirm` is neither `Secure` nor `__Host-`. Cookies are not port-scoped, so any page served from any other `localhost:*` origin can plant it and compute the matching `?confirm=` itself, walking through the CLI consent gate unseen.
samples.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable() = useSecureCookies() || loopbackCallback()` (github-auth.guard.ts:80-82). With `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/...`, `isSecureCookie()` returns false (oauth-state.ts:238), so `confirmCookieOptions().secure` is false (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:62) and `cliConfirmCookieName()` yields the bare `wafflebase_cli_confirm`. A page on `http://localhost:8080` (a compromised or hostile local dev server, or XSS in one) can run `document.cookie='wafflebase_cli_confirm=X; path=/'` — the cookie applies to `localhost:3000` because cookies ignore ports — then compute `cliConfirmToken('X', attackerPort, nonce, challenge)` (the helper is deterministic and its key is the cookie the attacker chose) and top-level navigate the victim to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker port>&nonce=…&challenge=…&confirm=<that HMAC>`. `Sec-Fetch-Site` for localhost→localhost is `same-site`, which `ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES` permits (github-auth.guard.ts:129), so `assertCliStartNotCrossSite` does not fire, `__cliConfirmed` is set at cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:158 with no page ever shown, and the backend mints an authorization code for the victim's GitHub account and redirects it to `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker port>/callback` (auth.controller.ts:212). The gate's own doc comment asserts the opposite ("positive evidence that the cookie can be *trusted*").

samples.summary: The `armLaunch` indirection does not actually keep the login bindings out of a local attacker's reach: the loopback launch URL that goes into `open()`'s argv is directly exchangeable for the full authorization URL (nonce + PKCE challenge) by anyone who can read argv.
samples.evidence: `armLaunch` returns `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<token>` (login.ts:826-830), which is what is passed to `deps.openBrowser(...)` (login.ts:351) and therefore what appears in the opener child's argv / `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. The handler at login.ts:654-671 answers the first GET with `302 Location: <authorization URL>`, so a local user who reads argv and curls it obtains `nonce` and `challenge` verbatim — the same secrets the indirection is documented as withholding (`docs/design/cli.md`: "The authorization URL never reaches argv or a log"). They can then complete GitHub consent in their own browser with those parameters and have the backend redirect a code for *their* account to the victim's still-listening `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` with the correct `state`, fixing the victim's CLI onto the attacker's account. Single use only makes the theft noisy (the victim's own browser gets the 410 page); it does not prevent it. Consider not putting a dereferenceable credential in argv at all (e.g. requiring a second secret the browser cannot supply, or binding the launch hit to a `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` + `Accept: text/html` shape).

samples.summary: `announceLoginUrl` writes a live login credential to `login-url.txt` with a non-exclusive, symlink-following write, into a directory created with default (umask) permissions, and leaves the file behind if the CLI is interrupted.
samples.evidence: login.ts:152-157 does `mkdirSync(dirname(file), {recursive:true})` (no `mode`, so the directory takes the process umask — potentially world-traversable when `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` points outside `$HOME`), then `rmSync(file, {force:true})` followed by `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode: 0o600})`. The default `w` flag follows symlinks and the rm→write window is a TOCTOU: in any directory another local user can write, an attacker pre-creating a symlink at that path receives the authorization URL (nonce + PKCE challenge) at a location they control, and the `0o600` applies to the followed target rather than protecting the secret. Prefer `flag: 'wx'` (or `openSync` with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW`) and `mkdirSync(..., {mode: 0o700})`. Separately, the `finally` at login.ts:361-366 only removes the file on normal completion — a `SIGINT` during the five-minute wait leaves a still-valid login URL on disk.

samples.summary: The docs added by this change advertise an `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` environment variable and an HKDF-derived signing key for the OAuth login bindings; no such variable, HKDF derivation or keyed MAC exists anywhere in the backend source.
samples.evidence: `docs/design/backend.md:757` and `packages/backend/README.md:25-34` describe `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` as "Key the OAuth login bindings are signed with… HKDF-derived from JWT_SECRET". A repo-wide grep for `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET`, `hkdf` and `bindingSecret` finds hits only in those two docs and in `docs/tasks/active/*-lessons.md`; `oauth-state.ts` binds the web state with an *unkeyed* `createHash('sha256')` (`hashSecret`, oauth-state.ts:266) and there is no keyed MAC over state at all. Operators reading these docs may believe they can rotate or isolate a key that has no effect, and may believe state is signed when it is only hashed.

samples.summary: `logSafeUrl`'s query redaction matches parameter names exactly, so array/bracket spellings that Express's `qs` parser still resolves to the same parameter (`?token[]=…`, `?token[0]=…`, `?token%5B%5D=…`) bypass it and land the credential in the access log verbatim.
samples.evidence: `redactParams` (log-safe-url.ts:131-147) tests `SENSITIVE_PARAMS.has(name.toLowerCase())` on the decoded raw name. `token[]` and `token[0]` are not members, so `GET /documents/abc/file?token[0]=<share token>` is logged in full; Express's default `qs` extended parsing turns that into `{token: ['…']}`, which reaches `@Query('token')` in `document-file.controller.ts:40` and 4xx/5xxs — i.e. the path that `customLogLevel` logs at `warn`/`error`. Same applies to the `SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS` rules, which require an exact segment count and so miss any spelling Express still routes with an extra empty or dot segment. Strip a trailing `[...]` from the name (or compare against the qs-parsed keys) before the membership test.

samples.summary: `clearAuthCookies`'s "every shape" sweep cannot actually expire a `__Host-`-prefixed cookie over the plain-http connection it was written for: a browser rejects a `__Host-` `Set-Cookie` that lacks `Secure`, so the non-`Secure` half of the sweep is a no-op for the prefixed names, and the stated "the non-Secure one overwrites and expires the Secure one" is false for them.
samples.evidence: auth.controller.ts:356-359 emits `res.clearCookie('__Host-wafflebase_session', {...base, secure:false})`. Per the cookie-prefix rules a UA must reject any `Set-Cookie` whose name starts with `__Host-` and that is not `Secure`, so that header is discarded; and the `secure:true` half is discarded on a plain-http connection. In the exact misconfiguration the doc comment cites (an origin served over http while `COOKIE_SECURE=true`/the config says otherwise), `POST /auth/logout` therefore answers 200 while the prefixed session and refresh cookies survive. The window is narrow (a `__Host-` cookie can normally only have been set over https), but the code and `docs/design/backend.md:437-446` both claim a completeness guarantee that does not hold.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:229-240) returns `false` for any `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starting `http://` at line 238, short-circuiting the `NODE_ENV === 'production'` fallback at line 239. That single answer is consumed by `baseCookieOptions()` via `useSecureCookies()` (auth.controller.ts:406), which is the only options source for the session cookie (auth.controller.ts:368) and refresh cookie (auth.controller.ts:376), and it also drives the cookie name through `hostPrefixedCookieName()` (oauth-state.ts:62-64, 89-95), so `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix are dropped together. The same value gates the OAuth-state cookie (oauth-state.ts:190), CLI-state cookie (oauth-state.ts:141) and CLI-confirm cookie (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:62). Operator docs do hand out non-loopback `http://` callback URLs (packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42 and :121, packages/backend/README.md:41), so a production self-host behind a TLS-terminating proxy that never re-pointed the callback URL emits session and refresh JWTs without `Secure` on an https origin, exposing them to any plaintext hop, and loses the sibling-subdomain write restriction. The only countermeasure in the tree is a log warning (`insecureProductionOrigin()`, github-auth.guard.ts:94-100) and prose (self-hosting.md:137-143); `COOKIE_SECURE=true` is opt-in. A warning does not make the vector unreachable, so `already-guarded` does not apply, and credential exposure via a weakened cookie flag is in the security lane. The source comment at oauth-state.ts:225-227 explicitly acknowledges this residual risk.

verdict.reason: Every claimed line checks out in the repo. cliLoginAvailable() is `useSecureCookies() || loopbackCallback()` (github-auth.guard.ts:80-82), and isSecureCookie() returns false for an http:// GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL (oauth-state.ts:238), so on a loopback deployment the CLI flow stays enabled while the consent cookie is issued without Secure and under the bare name `wafflebase_cli_confirm` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:62; oauth-state.ts:62-64). Because cookies are not port-scoped, script on any other origin on the same host (a hostile/XSS'd local dev server) can plant that cookie, and the confirm token is a deterministic HMAC keyed by the cookie value itself and recomputed from the request's own cookie/params (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:97-107, 139-150), so the attacker can pre-compute a matching ?confirm= and set __cliConfirmed at :158 without any page being shown. Sec-Fetch-Site for localhost:8080 -> localhost:3000 is `same-site`, which ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES permits (github-auth.guard.ts:129, 309-319), so assertCliStartNotCrossSite does not fire; the guard then mints CLI state (github-auth.guard.ts:209-220) and the callback delivers the victim's code to http://127.0.0.1:<attacker port>/callback (auth.controller.ts:212-214), redeemable via /auth/cli/exchange with the attacker's own verifier (auth.controller.ts:244-259) since the attacker chose the challenge. The cliState browser-binding cookie (oauth-state.ts:128-150; auth.controller.ts:180-186) does not guard this path because the victim's own browser performs the navigation and therefore holds the matching secret. This is an in-lane consent/authorization bypass, so no refutation ground applies; the local-origin prerequisite lowers likelihood, not reality.

finding.summary: Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: review: every credential in the pool (2) was retired — nothing left to fail over to

verdict.reason:
The "finding" contains no code claim at all — no file, no line, no described vector. Its text is verbatim the runtime error string the review harness itself emits when its own Anthropic credential pool drains: `poolExhaustedError` at scripts/agent/ask.mjs:630-637 builds `"${label}: every credential in the pool (${pool.size}) was retired — nothing left to fail over to"`, thrown from the failover path at scripts/agent/ask.mjs:693 and the pre-session gate at scripts/agent/ask.mjs:743. The prefix "Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict:" means the upstream reviewer agent aborted mid-run (all credentials retired) and emitted its own operational error in place of a review, so there is no asserted defect in this repository to verify.

I checked the cited code for any security substance of its own and found none in my lane: the message is intentionally constructed to carry only a lens label and an integer count (`pool.size`) — no token, key, or credential material is interpolated (scripts/agent/ask.mjs:631-632), and the surrounding documentation at scripts/agent/ask.mjs:607-628 shows the wording is deliberately non-specific about WHY a slot retired. The behaviour is covered by scripts/agent/ask.test.mjs:295-301 as intended behaviour, not a bug. That is not an authorization gate, secret exposure, injection sink, or crypto check, so even read charitably as a claim about ask.mjs it is not a Security-lens defect.

Ground: not-present — the asserted defect does not exist as described (nothing is described); the quoted string is an intended diagnostic in the harness, produced because the reviewer process ran out of API credentials.
